title: Labor Rights Are Human Rights
author: Meizhu Lui
content:
_This article by Meizhu Lui originally appeared in the[September 23, 2026
edition of the Mexico Solidarity
Bulletin](https://mexicosolidarityproject.substack.com/p/mexico-solidarity-
bulletin-92326), a weekly publication of the Mexico Solidarity Project._

_Subscribe[here](https://mexicosolidarityproject.com/subscribe-contact/) to
receive original content and a Mexico news compilation weekly._

What's the foundational human right? **The right to work and to make or grow
as much as you need to live with dignity and security.** From that right,
other rights follow—to housing, to food, to mobility and so on.

In 1994, the NAFTA free trade agreement—negotiated in a neoliberal
framework—took away that basic natural right in favor of corporate rights. It
was foreign corporations that got the freedom to migrate, resulting in the
many human rights violations we suffer today. In Mexico, we've seen
displacement and worker migration, water and air pollution, and loss of access
to safe drinking water; in the US, we've lost industrial jobs, which has often
resulted in depressed workers with increased suicides and drug abuse, in turn
creating a market for drugs with the rise of the drug cartels and expanding
gun trade.

In 2018, the USMCA, or T-MEC, continued that agreement, with US unions
demanding and getting some improvements for workers. The new Labor Accords
specifically supported **the right of workers to form democratic, independent
unions in Mexico** , giving workers the hope of getting rid of corrupt
_charro_ unions and gaining the power to win better wages and working
conditions. In 2019, Mexican labor reform put that right into law.

Workers did begin to organize independent unions. But companies never wanted
to enforce the labor reforms of 2019—so repression and violence against the
labor organizers continued; it simply took a different form. Under the PRI/PAN
governments, the state perpetrated the repression and persecution of union
leaders, including firing on demonstrators. That's no longer true. **Now, the
companies hire thugs, some connected to cartels, to intimidate workers.**

But even though the United Nations and the International Labor Organization
recognize labor rights as human rights, **Mexico does not.**

The [new report](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1vWq16BsCymqAXXkgzotXaq_pMs-
INplu/view) to Mexico's _Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos_ (CNDH)
makes a strong case for changing that and for new protocols to protect those
who are exercising their right to form unions.
